title: Miniature giants: investigating limb long bone structure in dwarf proboscideans
summary: Terrestrial vertebrates rely on their skeleton to provide structural support and allow the movement of the body. Heavy, graviportal taxa, such as extant elephants, exhibit numerous adaptive features in their bone anatomy enabling them to withstand their immense weight. Conversely, dwarfing events impose novel biomechanical constraints on the skeleton. The case of dwarf elephants raises the question of how graviportal animals adapt when undergoing drastic size reduction, and whether they retain graviportal features or exhibit paedomorphic traits. In this study, we examine the morphology and microanatomy of the six long bones in two fossil species of dwarf elephants, Palaeoloxodon tiliensis (adults) and P.___falconeri (juveniles), using both quantitative and qualitative approaches (3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, compact bone thickness cartographies). Our results show that in P.___tiliensis , the reduction in body mass is reflected in the morphology and microanatomy of the bones, suggesting a more flexed limb posture and a reduced parasagittal orientation compared to in fully graviportal proboscideans. Despite this shift, several key graviportal adaptations are retained in P.___tiliensis . Additionally, comparisons with early, non-graviportal proboscideans indicate that dwarf elephants exhibit a partial reversion to ancestral limb traits, while maintaining essential weight-bearing features. Finally, adult P.___tiliensis and juvenile P.___falconeri specimens exhibit a medullary area filled with trabecular bone, similar to that of extant elephants. Dwarf elephants are thus not scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors, but instead display a combination of juvenile, graviportal and ancestral traits reflecting the impact of dwarfism on their evolutionary trajectory.

AI.tldr: This study examines the morphology and microanatomy of long bones in two fossil dwarf elephant species (Palaeoloxodon tiliensis and P. falconeri) using 3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, and compact bone thickness cartographies. Results show that dwarf elephants retain key graviportal features while partially reverting to ancestral limb traits and exhibiting juvenile characteristics, indicating they are not simply scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors.
AI.motivation: To understand how graviportal animals adapt biomechanically when undergoing drastic size reduction (dwarfing), specifically whether dwarf elephants retain graviportal features or exhibit paedomorphic traits.
AI.method: Quantitative and qualitative analyses of six long bones from two fossil dwarf elephant species using 3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, and compact bone thickness cartographies.
AI.result: P. tiliensis shows reduced body mass reflected in bone morphology suggesting more flexed limb posture and reduced parasagittal orientation, yet retains several graviportal adaptations. Dwarf elephants exhibit partial reversion to ancestral limb traits while maintaining weight-bearing features. Both adult P. tiliensis and juvenile P. falconeri display medullary areas filled with trabecular bone similar to extant elephants.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf elephants are not scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors but display a combination of juvenile, graviportal, and ancestral traits reflecting the impact of dwarfism on their evolutionary trajectory.

title: The Connectome and the Quest for the Functional Logic of the Drosophila Early Olfactory System
summary: In recent decades, the early olfactory system (EOS) of the fruit fly has become a leading model for studying olfactory processing and associative memory, owing in part to a well-characterized feedforward pathway that feeds the processes underlying associative memory and by examining the role played by a handful of neurons and synapses. The recent completion of dense electron-microscopy connectomes provides high quality visualizations of every cell type, neuron, and synapse along the early olfactory pathway. Yet a wiring diagram, however complete, does not by itself reveal the functional logic of a neural circuit. Reviewing the EOS connectome and synaptome datasets of the past fifteen years, we note that the feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits of large scale multi-input multi-output neurons. A systematic understanding of feedback loop abstractions, and their capacity to govern the input/output transformations at each neuropil stage, is the underlying foundation of the functional logic of the early olfactory circuits. In addition, we argue that a quantitative account of the functional logic requires an explicit model of the odorants present in the natural environment. Consisting of odorant objects, such a model defines the semantics and syntax of olfactory information processing, and calls for new distance measures for classifying the odorant semantics in support of associative memory operations. Furthermore, odor information processing must abide by causality, treating the circuit as a real-time, stage-by-stage cascade of giant local feedback loops.

AI.tldr: This review analyzes the fruit fly early olfactory system (EOS) connectome and synaptome data, arguing that the well-studied feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits of large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons. The authors contend that understanding these feedback loops is essential to uncovering the functional logic of olfactory circuits, and that a complete account requires an explicit model of natural odorants, new distance measures for odorant semantics, and a causality-respecting, stage-by-stage cascade treatment of the circuit.
AI.motivation: Although dense electron-microscopy connectomes now provide complete wiring diagrams of the early olfactory pathway, a static wiring diagram alone does not reveal the functional logic of a neural circuit. The authors seek to bridge this gap by examining the feedback architectures embedded within the feedforward pathway and emphasizing the need for natural odorant models and causality-aware processing.
AI.method: The paper reviews fifteen years of EOS connectome and synaptome datasets, identifies that the feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits involving large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons, and proposes a framework for understanding feedback loop abstractions and their role in governing input/output transformations at each neuropil stage. It also advocates for explicit modeling of natural odorant objects, new distance measures for odorant semantics, and a causality-respecting cascade view of the circuit.
AI.result: The review finds that the early olfactory system is dominated by dense local feedback circuits rather than a purely feedforward architecture, and argues that feedback loop abstractions provide the foundation for understanding functional logic. It also concludes that quantitative understanding requires models of natural odorant environments, novel semantic distance measures, and causality-aware stage-by-stage processing.
AI.conclusion: The functional logic of the fruit fly early olfactory circuit cannot be inferred from the wiring diagram alone; it requires systematic abstraction of local feedback loops, an explicit model of natural odorant objects and semantics, and a treatment of the circuit as a real-time, causal cascade of giant local feedback loops.

title: Reducing Boolean Networks via Analysis of Dynamic Network Subgraph Behavior
comment: 33 pages, 6 figures, Check this Github repository for codes and more detials: https://github.com/jafarilab/BORNA
summary: Boolean networks provide a compact framework for modeling regulatory systems, yet their rapidly expanding state spaces make systematic dynamical analysis challenging. Here, we systematically enumerate all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory subgraphs with their admissible Boolean update rules and exhaustively characterize their state-transition graphs (STGs) under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. By extracting quantitative dynamical descriptors, we move beyond static wiring diagrams toward a behavior-based classification of network structures. The synchronous analysis identifies deterministic fixed-point and cyclic attractor regimes, while the asynchronous analysis captures one-node-at-a-time dynamics through terminal strongly connected components of the asynchronous STGs. Comparing the two update schemes distinguishes dynamical behaviors that are robust across update assumptions from those that depend on synchronous updating. Despite the diversity of graph-rule combinations, many realizations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes, revealing substantial redundancy between structural and dynamical representations. We further propose a testable framework for investigating whether such local dynamical classes can be used to characterize selected subnetworks within larger Boolean models. To facilitate exploration and reproducibility, we developed BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the complete network catalogue, STGs, and synchronous and asynchronous simulations, available at https://jafarilab.github.io/BORNA/. Together, these results provide a systematic reference for minimal Boolean network dynamics and a foundation for extending behavior-based analysis to larger regulatory systems.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically enumerates all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory Boolean networks and exhaustively characterizes their state-transition graphs under both synchronous and asynchronous updating, revealing that diverse graph-rule combinations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes. The authors introduce BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the complete catalogue, and propose a framework for using local dynamical classes to characterize subnetworks in larger Boolean models.
AI.motivation: Boolean networks compactly model regulatory systems, but their rapidly expanding state spaces make systematic dynamical analysis challenging. The authors aim to move beyond static wiring diagrams toward behavior-based classification of network structures by exhaustively characterizing minimal (two-node) network dynamics under both update schemes.
AI.method: The authors enumerate all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory subgraphs with admissible Boolean update rules, then exhaustively analyze their state-transition graphs (STGs) under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. They extract quantitative dynamical descriptors (fixed points, cyclic attractors, terminal strongly connected components) and compare the two update schemes to identify robust vs. update-dependent behaviors. They also built BORNA, a web application for exploration and simulation.
AI.result: Despite the diversity of graph-rule combinations, many realizations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes, revealing substantial redundancy between structural and dynamical representations. The synchronous analysis identifies deterministic fixed-point and cyclic attractor regimes, while asynchronous analysis captures one-node-at-a-time dynamics through terminal strongly connected components. Comparisons distinguish update-robust behaviors from synchronous-dependent ones.
AI.conclusion: The authors provide a systematic reference for minimal Boolean network dynamics, propose a testable framework for using local dynamical classes to characterize subnetworks within larger Boolean models, and offer BORNA as a reproducible, interactive tool. This lays a foundation for extending behavior-based analysis to larger regulatory systems.

authors: Isabel M. V. Guedes de Carvalho
title: Hepatitis C Virus Genotyping with a Transformer Neural Network
summary: This study aims to explore the applicability of Transformer-based models for genetic sequence classification by evaluating their performance in predicting hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotypes and subtypes after fine-tuning. A total of 2,881 HCV whole-genome sequences obtained from the Los Alamos HCV Sequence Database were used, including genotypes 1 to 6 and all confirmed subtypes. Genotypes 7 and 8 were excluded due to an insufficient number of samples. The fine-tuning process was based on several datasets that differed in fragmentation method, data volume per file, and labeling. In genotype classification, fine-tuning strategies employing homogeneous fragmentation and balanced sample distribution resulted in higher performance, with precision ranging from 98.48% to 100%. In contrast, fine-tuning conducted using a fragmentation strategy that caused data imbalance, along with an arbitrary distribution of samples across training files, achieved a precision of 48.12%, which is considered low compared with other models. This configuration, which was also manually evaluated, resulted in a high error rate in genotype 5 prediction due to its low frequency in the datasets used. In subtype classification, the best-performing fine-tuning approach achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision. Models that included additional genotypes showed a slight decrease in performance due to the increased complexity of the task. This study demonstrates that, when fine-tuning datasets contain properly fragmented, distributed, and labeled genetic sequences, Transformer-based neural networks can achieve high performance and are a promising approach for HCV genotype and subtype classification.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates fine-tuned Transformer-based models for HCV genotype and subtype classification using 2,881 whole-genome sequences. With proper data fragmentation and balanced distribution, models achieved 98.48-100% precision for genotype prediction and 99.89% accuracy for subtype classification, while poor fragmentation strategies caused significant performance drops (48.12% precision).
AI.motivation: To explore whether Transformer-based models can be effectively applied to genetic sequence classification tasks, specifically for predicting hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotypes and subtypes through fine-tuning, while examining how data preparation strategies impact model performance.
AI.method: Fine-tuned Transformer-based models on 2,881 HCV whole-genome sequences from the Los Alamos HCV Sequence Database (genotypes 1-6). Multiple fine-tuning configurations were tested, varying in fragmentation method, data volume per file, and labeling strategy, including balanced vs. imbalanced sample distributions.
AI.result: Homogeneous fragmentation with balanced sample distribution achieved 98.48-100% precision in genotype classification, while imbalanced fragmentation produced only 48.12% precision. For subtype classification, the best model achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision. Including additional genotypes slightly decreased performance due to increased task complexity.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based neural networks are a promising approach for HCV genotype and subtype classification, provided that fine-tuning datasets are properly fragmented, distributed, and labeled with balanced sample representation across training files.

title: A stochastic dose-response framework for environmentally persistent pathogens
summary: Infectious diseases caused by environmentally persistent pathogens can strongly affect host populations as transmission occurs not only through direct host-host contact but also via indirect exposure to contaminated environments. While in some systems environmental reservoirs help sustain exposure even when infected host numbers are low, reliance on environmental transmission pathway may also increase pathogen extinction risk. Infection risk may depend on both pathogen dose and timing of exposure. Thus, understanding how dose-response, stochasticity, and seasonal changes in host susceptibility or contact rates shape pathogen invasion and persistence remains an important challenge for environmentally transmitted disease systems. To address this, we develop a stochastic dose-response framework that integrates host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir. Transmission occurs through both direct contact with infectious hosts and indirect environmental exposure, with infection probability governed by dose-response functions. We focus on stochastic continuous-time Markov chain formulation and use branching process approximation to estimate disease extinction probabilities when infected hosts or environmental pathogen loads are low. We extend the framework to include seasonality in host susceptibility, environmental contact, and host-host contact. As a case study, we apply the model to snake fungal disease. Numerical simulations show that dose-response influences epidemic takeoff and infection levels, while seasonality creates windows of high and low extinction risk. These extinction risks depend strongly on the route and timing of introduction within the seasonal cycle. These results, coupled with global sensitivity analysis, illustrate how stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing shape outbreak dynamics for environmentally persistent pathogens.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a stochastic dose-response framework integrating host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir, incorporating both direct and indirect transmission pathways, seasonality, and branching process approximations to estimate disease extinction probabilities. Applied to snake fungal disease, the model shows that dose-response shapes epidemic dynamics while seasonality creates windows of varying extinction risk depending on introduction route and timing.
AI.motivation: Environmentally persistent pathogens present a unique challenge because transmission occurs via both direct host-host contact and indirect exposure to contaminated environments. Understanding how dose-response relationships, stochasticity, and seasonal variation in host susceptibility or contact rates influence pathogen invasion and persistence is critical but remains poorly understood for environmentally transmitted disease systems.
AI.method: The study develops a stochastic continuous-time Markov chain framework that integrates host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir. Transmission is modeled through both direct contact with infectious hosts and indirect environmental exposure, with infection probability governed by dose-response functions. Branching process approximations estimate extinction probabilities when infected hosts or environmental pathogen loads are low. The framework is extended to incorporate seasonality in host susceptibility, environmental contact, and host-host contact, and applied to snake fungal disease as a case study.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate that dose-response functions influence epidemic takeoff and infection levels, while seasonality creates windows of high and low extinction risk. Extinction risks depend strongly on the route and timing of pathogen introduction within the seasonal cycle. Global sensitivity analysis reveals how stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing collectively shape outbreak dynamics for environmentally persistent pathogens.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight that stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing jointly determine outbreak dynamics for environmentally persistent pathogens, providing a framework that can inform understanding of invasion and persistence risks in these disease systems.

title: Correlations at criticality in ecological communities
summary: Ecological communities are continually reshaped by invasion, exclusion, and diversification, processes that naturally drive them toward the boundary of dynamical stability. Near such a boundary, a soft mode relaxes increasingly slowly and, under stochastic forcing, is expected to dominate the fluctuations, effectively reducing the dynamics to one dimension and generating strong positive and negative abundance correlations. Such correlations have therefore been proposed as signatures of an imminent transition. Here we show that this expectation can fail even arbitrarily close to criticality. The reason is that spectral softness does not guarantee stochastic visibility: the soft mode must receive enough environmental forcing to dominate the fluctuation background generated by the remaining modes. We demonstrate this mechanism in three ecological scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, a local community assembled by immigration from a regional pool, and a community generated by repeated diversification. In all three, communities approach marginal stability without developing the near-perfect pairwise correlations predicted by the single-mode picture. Thus, proximity to ecological criticality need not be visible in equal-time pairwise correlations.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the assumption that near-critical ecological communities inevitably exhibit strong pairwise abundance correlations. Using three ecological scenarios, the authors demonstrate that spectral softness does not guarantee stochastic visibility—the soft mode must receive sufficient environmental forcing to dominate fluctuations. Thus, proximity to criticality may not be detectable in equal-time pairwise correlations.
AI.motivation: Ecological communities are thought to approach dynamical stability boundaries, where soft modes should dominate fluctuations and generate strong abundance correlations. These correlations have been proposed as early-warning signatures of imminent ecological transitions. The authors aim to test whether this prediction holds universally.
AI.method: The authors analyze the dynamics of ecological communities near marginal stability using stochastic forcing. They examine three scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, a local community assembled by immigration from a regional pool, and a community generated by repeated diversification. They assess whether soft modes become stochastically visible (i.e., dominate fluctuations) in each case.
AI.result: The expectation that near-critical communities develop strong pairwise correlations fails even arbitrarily close to criticality. In all three ecological scenarios, communities approach marginal stability without producing the near-perfect pairwise correlations predicted by the single-mode picture, because the soft mode does not receive enough environmental forcing to dominate the fluctuation background from remaining modes.
AI.conclusion: Proximity to ecological criticality need not be visible in equal-time pairwise correlations. Spectral softness is insufficient for detecting imminent transitions; the stochastic visibility of soft modes depends on how environmental forcing projects onto them. This has important implications for using correlation-based early-warning signals in ecology.

title: PEtab SciML: an exchange format for specifying and training dynamic scientific machine learning models
summary: Summary: Dynamic scientific machine learning (SciML) models that combine mechanistic ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with machine learning (ML) components have applications ranging from learning unknown biological processes to integrating auxiliary data modalities into dynamic modelling. To enable reproducible and efficient SciML training, we introduce PEtab SciML, an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems in which mechanistic and ML model parameters are jointly estimated from time series data. PEtab SciML supports several ML ODE hybridization patterns in realistic problem setups. It is accompanied by a reference Python library and downstream modelling support in Python/JAX and Julia, provided by AMICI and PEtab.jl, respectively, and a collection of real data benchmarks. Availability and implementation: PEtab SciML is available on GitHub (https://github.com/PEtab-dev/petab_sciml). The reference Python package is installable from PyPI and is continuously tested and supported on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

AI.tldr: PEtab SciML is an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems where mechanistic ODE models and machine learning components are jointly trained from time series data, accompanied by a Python reference library and support in Python/JAX and Julia ecosystems.
AI.motivation: Dynamic scientific machine learning (SciML) models that combine mechanistic ODEs with ML components have broad applications, but there is a lack of reproducible and efficient standards for specifying and solving parameter estimation problems in such hybrid models.
AI.method: The paper introduces PEtab SciML, an interoperable data format for specifying joint parameter estimation problems of mechanistic and ML model parameters, supporting multiple ML-ODE hybridization patterns in realistic setups, with a reference Python library and downstream support via AMICI (Python/JAX) and PEtab.jl (Julia), plus real data benchmarks.
AI.result: The format and tooling provide a reproducible and efficient workflow for SciML training, with continuous testing and support across Linux, macOS, and Windows, and availability on PyPI and GitHub.
AI.conclusion: PEtab SciML fills a gap in the SciML ecosystem by providing an interoperable, standardized format for hybrid mechanistic-ML parameter estimation, promoting reproducibility and cross-language usability.

title: Novel models of trait evolution via an expansion of Lande's fitness function: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process meets the Little Prince's boa
comment: Submitted to the Journal of the Society of Modeling and Theory in Population Biology
summary: Adaptive topographies form the foundation for much of our understanding of evolutionary change. Lande's 1976 influential paper on the adaptive topography of phenotypes demonstrated how the concept is inherent in both phenotypic and genetic models of evolution, and how the concept can be used to test evolutionary hypotheses given data. Here, we revisit and generalize Lande's original derivation of an equation analogous to Wright's genotypic adaptive topography to the case of two fitness components. A move to two fitness components yields novel predictions about the shape and mechanistic underpinnings of the adaptive topography. The optimum of this updated fitness function is a weighted average of the optima of the two fitness components, with weights given by the relative strengths of stabilizing selection on each component. Temporal or spatial heterogeneity in the strengths of selection for each fitness component create novel shapes (asymmetry, bi-modality, or lack thereof) of the overall fitness function, a possibility demonstrated with a case-study from the published literature. Finally, when combined with Lande's approach to generate an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model for the evolution of the average phenotype, our fitness formulation leads to a previously unrecognized family of stochastic differential equation models of trait evolution. These results provide mechanistic justification for non-Gaussian fitness functions (often observed in natural systems), provide a path for testing alternative models generating non-Gaussian fitness functions, and pave the way for future study of the interplay of ecological and evolutionary dynamics, such as in the study of evolutionary rescue.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes Lande's 1976 adaptive topography framework from a single fitness component to two fitness components. The extended model shows the overall fitness optimum is a weighted average of component optima, where weights reflect relative strengths of stabilizing selection. The authors demonstrate that temporally or spatially varying selection strengths can generate asymmetric or bimodal fitness functions, and this formulation leads to a new family of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic differential equation models for trait evolution.
AI.motivation: Adaptive topographies are foundational to evolutionary theory, but Lande's original framework assumed a single (typically Gaussian) fitness component. Many natural systems exhibit non-Gaussian fitness functions, and extending the theory to multiple fitness components could provide mechanistic justification and testable predictions for these observations.
AI.method: The authors revisit and generalize Lande's derivation of the phenotypic adaptive topography equation to the case of two fitness components. They derive the updated fitness function, analyze its shape properties (symmetry, bimodality) under varying selection strengths, illustrate with a published case study, and extend Lande's approach to generate new OU-type stochastic differential equation models.
AI.result: The two-component generalization yields a fitness optimum that is a weighted average of component optima, weighted by relative stabilizing selection strengths. Heterogeneous selection strengths across time or space can produce novel fitness landscape shapes (asymmetry, bimodality). This formulation also generates a previously unrecognized family of stochastic differential equation models for trait evolution.
AI.conclusion: The generalized framework provides mechanistic justification for non-Gaussian fitness functions, offers a pathway for testing alternative models that generate such functions, and opens avenues for studying eco-evolutionary dynamics such as evolutionary rescue.

title: Automatic bioinformatic software named entity recognition from literature
summary: Bioinformatics software and databases are essential components of modern life science research, yet their mentions in the scientific literature are often inconsistent and difficult to systematically identify at scale. The lack of a comprehensive and up-to-date catalog of bioinformatics resources hinders efforts toward automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis. Here we present SNAIL, a hybrid named entity recognition framework designed to automatically identify bioinformatics software and database (SW/DB) names from biomedical texts. SNAIL integrates complementary lexical and semantic modeling strategies. The lexical component captures orthographic patterns and contextual cues characteristic of SW/DB names, while the semantic component leverages contextual embeddings generated by transformer-based language models such as SciBERT, combined with an explicit token-masking strategy to enhance entity-focused representations. A large training corpus was constructed automatically through a hybrid pipeline that integrates citation-hinted extraction with large language model-assisted distillation. Evaluation on two independent benchmark datasets and real-world research articles demonstrates that SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches, including domain-specific methods such as bioNerDS2 and general-purpose large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude. Applying SNAIL to large-scale literature analysis further reveals distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields. These results demonstrate that SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts and enables systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

AI.tldr: SNAIL is a hybrid named entity recognition framework that automatically identifies bioinformatics software and database (SW/DB) names from biomedical texts by integrating lexical pattern matching with transformer-based semantic embeddings (e.g., SciBERT) and a token-masking strategy. It was trained on a large automatically constructed corpus and outperforms existing methods including bioNerDS2 and general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude), enabling large-scale meta-analysis of tool usage across bioinformatics subfields.
AI.motivation: Bioinformatics software and database mentions in scientific literature are inconsistent and difficult to identify at scale, and no comprehensive up-to-date catalog exists, hindering automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis.
AI.method: SNAIL combines a lexical component (capturing orthographic patterns and contextual cues of SW/DB names) with a semantic component using transformer-based contextual embeddings (SciBERT) plus an explicit token-masking strategy. A large training corpus was built via a hybrid pipeline integrating citation-hinted extraction with LLM-assisted distillation.
AI.result: SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches—including domain-specific bioNerDS2 and general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude)—on two benchmark datasets and real-world articles. Large-scale application revealed distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields.
AI.conclusion: SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts, enabling systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

title: Quantum Kernel Estimation for the Discovery of Early Lung Cancer Detection
summary:
Lung cancer screening with low-dose chest computed tomography reduces mortality, but its impact is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cell-free DNA (cfDNA) biomarkers offer a complementary approach, although early detection remains difficult because of lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. We evaluated quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using DNA fragmentomics and DNA methylation. After feature selection, models were trained using 20- and 40-feature subsets. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed with exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression and compared with an SVM model trained on the original features.
  This framework enabled systematic evaluation of how encoding and entanglement design affect classification. Across repeated held-out evaluations, quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC relative to a classical SVM baseline, suggesting effective capture of nonlinear cfDNA fragmentation structure. For methylation, the classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, although selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability. Overall, these results support quantum kernel methods as a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentomics and methylation biomarkers. Quantum kernel models (using angle/dense-angle feature maps with various entanglement strategies) achieved competitive performance against classical SVM baselines, with some 20-feature fragmentomics configurations improving AUC, while increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently help.
AI.motivation: Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT reduces mortality but is limited by low uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cfDNA biomarkers offer a complementary approach, but early detection is difficult due to lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. Quantum-classical hybrid machine learning could potentially capture these nonlinear patterns better than classical methods.
AI.method: cfDNA fragmentomics and methylation data were used. After feature selection, 20- and 40-feature subsets were trained. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed via exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression, compared against an SVM trained on original features.
AI.result: Quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance across repeated held-out evaluations. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC over classical SVM baseline. For methylation, classical SVM achieved highest AUC, though select quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum kernel methods are a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection, particularly for capturing nonlinear fragmentomic structure with smaller feature sets. The framework enables systematic evaluation of encoding and entanglement design, though larger feature counts do not necessarily yield better performance.

title: Longitudinal Bayesian Learning of Continuous Disease Position across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses as a continuous biological process, whereas most existing neuroimaging-based artificial intelligence methods remain limited to discrete diagnosis or clinical score prediction from cross-sectional imaging. In this work, we propose Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that continuously estimates disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Specifically, DCP models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal observations with weak clinical supervision, from which the proposed Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived to quantify an individual's position along the Alzheimer's disease continuum together with its associated uncertainty. Extensive experiments on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort demonstrate that DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. More importantly, comprehensive validation analyses show that DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion. These results suggest that DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that continuously estimates Alzheimer's disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging by modeling disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable, yielding a Disease Continuum Score (DCS) with uncertainty quantification that outperforms existing methods on ADNI.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease progresses as a continuous biological process, yet existing neuroimaging-based AI methods are limited to discrete diagnosis or cross-sectional clinical score prediction, failing to capture the continuous nature of disease progression.
AI.method: DCP is a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable, jointly integrating longitudinal DTI observations with weak clinical supervision to derive a Disease Continuum Score (DCS) that quantifies an individual's position along the AD continuum with associated uncertainty.
AI.result: On the ADNI cohort, DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. Validation analyses show DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion.
AI.conclusion: DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression, going beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

title: Resource-Efficient Bio-Molecular Docking on a NISQ-era Digital Quantum Computer
summary: Molecular docking is a vital computational task in drug discovery, wherein the objective is to efficiently identify optimal binding poses between a ligand and a target receptor protein. Due to the combinatorial explosion of possible binding configurations, docking of large and flexible molecules remains a computationally intensive problem, especially at scale. Early studies have revealed that the molecular docking can be re-cast as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) problem on a compatibility graph to be solved classically. In this work, we proposed a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking leveraging the MVWCP formalism with a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy, which enables efficient encoding of classical binary variables with Bloch sphere vectors. We further prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be chosen to be a pure product state, thereby providing a rigorous justification for its optimization using a unitary variational circuit. The molecular docking problem is first mapped to a cost Hamiltonian that is minimized within a variational framework, optimized via a randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm start, and gradient-based techniques. Finally, we also executed the circuit on an IBM quantum computer, underlying the feasibility and of quantum-assisted optimization for structure-based drug design and point towards the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques in quantum optimization for computational biology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking by reformulating it as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) and solving it with a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy on quantum hardware, demonstrating feasibility on an IBM quantum computer.
AI.motivation: Molecular docking is computationally intensive due to the combinatorial explosion of binding configurations, especially for large and flexible molecules at scale. Existing classical methods struggle with this complexity, motivating the exploration of quantum-assisted approaches for more efficient structure-based drug design.
AI.method: The molecular docking problem is mapped to a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) on a compatibility graph, then re-formulated as a cost Hamiltonian minimization. A variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy encodes classical binary variables using Bloch sphere vectors. The optimization uses a randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm start combined with gradient-based techniques, and the circuit is executed on an IBM quantum computer.
AI.result: The authors prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be chosen as a pure product state, providing rigorous justification for optimizing it with a unitary variational circuit. The circuit execution on IBM quantum hardware demonstrates the feasibility of quantum-assisted optimization for molecular docking.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes the viability of quantum-assisted optimization for structure-based drug design and highlights the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques in quantum optimization applied to computational biology.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Brain Researcher is an agentic research harness that enforces admissible analyses, required checks, and claim-scope rules within a neuroimaging computational environment, improving tool-selection accuracy and verifiable grounding while enabling multiverse analyses and structured scientific review of claims.
AI.motivation: AI agents can produce analytic outputs but often fail to convert them into defensible scientific claims—they exhibit selective analysis, premature success declarations, and optimization of imperfect criteria. The paper aims to embed methodological rigor directly into the agentic workflow rather than applying it post hoc.
AI.method: Brain Researcher operates inside a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under explicit rules governing admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope. It includes multiverse analyses to expose analytic-choice sensitivity and a scientific review process that classifies claims into categories such as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected, or deferred.
AI.result: Across seven models, Brain Researcher improved first-choice tool-selection accuracy by 70.2 percentage points (from 23.3% to 93.6%) and increased verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. Collaborator-led and self-evolving studies demonstrated that multiverse analyses revealed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review effectively classified claims.
AI.conclusion: By linking decisions to evidence and provenance and embedding methodological judgment within the workflow, Brain Researcher transforms agentic outputs into defensible scientific claims, addressing reproducibility and rigor challenges in AI-driven research.

title: Flow Matching Meets 3D Curvilinear Structure Segmentation in Medical Imaging
comment: International Workshop on Machine Learning in Medical Imaging (MLMI 2026) @ MICCAI
summary: Segmentation of curvilinear anatomical structures in 3D medical images remains challenging due to complex topology, severe class imbalance, weak contrast, and large variations in structure morphology. While deep learning approaches for 3D curvilinear segmentation have been proposed, they are often tailored to specific anatomies or modalities, limiting generalization across clinical settings and leaving room for improvement. Recent generative models have shown the benefits of iterative prediction for structured segmentation tasks, yet diffusion-based methods suffer from computationally expensive sampling, hindering their use on high-resolution 3D volumes. We present 3D-CurvSegFlow, a flow matching-based model for 3D curvilinear structure segmentation. The model learns a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to the target vascular representation, enabling progressive refinement of complex curvilinear geometries with efficient inference. We evaluate our method on Three public challenging datasets covering distinct anatomies and modalities: portal vein, cerebral vessel, and coronary arteries. Using a common architecture and training strategy across all tasks, our method outperforms general-purpose and vessel-specific approaches, with strong preservation of thin branches and vascular continuity. This work not only advances the state-of-the-art in 3D curvilinear segmentation but also opens new avenues for efficient, generalizable, and clinically applicable methods in medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: 3D-CurvSegFlow is a flow matching-based deep learning model for segmenting curvilinear anatomical structures (e.g., vessels) in 3D medical images, achieving state-of-the-art performance across three diverse public datasets (portal vein, cerebral vessels, coronary arteries) with a single unified architecture and training strategy.
AI.motivation: 3D curvilinear structure segmentation is challenging due to complex topology, class imbalance, weak contrast, and morphological variation. Existing deep learning methods are often anatomy- or modality-specific, and diffusion-based generative approaches are computationally expensive for high-resolution 3D volumes.
AI.method: The paper presents 3D-CurvSegFlow, a flow matching-based generative model that learns a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to the target vascular representation, enabling progressive refinement of curvilinear geometries with efficient inference.
AI.result: Using a common architecture and training strategy across three public datasets (portal vein, cerebral vessel, coronary arteries), the method outperforms both general-purpose and vessel-specific segmentation approaches, with strong preservation of thin branches and vascular continuity.
AI.conclusion: The work advances state-of-the-art in 3D curvilinear segmentation and demonstrates efficient, generalizable, and clinically applicable generative methods for medical image analysis.

title: Emergence of cooperation: A reputation-modulated reinforcement learning
summary: Reputation is widely recognized as a key mechanism for sustaining cooperation. However, most existing game-theoretic models treat reputation primarily as an external factor that modulates payoffs, interaction structures, or strategy update rules. In many social contexts, though, reputation operates primarily as information -- it shapes how individuals interpret their own experiences and assess the behavior of others. To bridge this gap, we propose a spatial prisoner's dilemma game grounded in the reinforcement learning paradigm, in which agents equipped with Q-learning integrate both individual and social information via a locally defined reputation metric to guide their decisions. Our results reveal that reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes the emergence of cooperative behavior, and we observe a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection as the temptation increases. Cooperation spreads through the nucleation of cooperative clusters, whereas the disintegration of these clusters drives the system into an absorbing state of complete defection. Overall, this study demonstrates that reputation facilitates cooperation not only by providing direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a spatial prisoner's dilemma game where agents use Q-learning (reinforcement learning) combined with a locally defined reputation metric to integrate individual and social information. Results show reputation-modulated learning promotes cooperation, with a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection as temptation increases, driven by nucleation and disintegration of cooperative clusters.
AI.motivation: Existing game-theoretic models treat reputation mainly as an external factor modulating payoffs, interaction structures, or strategy update rules. However, in many social contexts, reputation operates primarily as information that shapes how individuals interpret their experiences and assess others' behavior—a gap this paper aims to bridge.
AI.method: The authors develop a spatial prisoner's dilemma game grounded in reinforcement learning, where agents equipped with Q-learning integrate both individual and social information through a locally defined reputation metric to guide their decision-making.
AI.result: Reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes cooperation. A discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection is observed as temptation increases. Cooperation propagates via nucleation of cooperative clusters, while disintegration of these clusters leads to an absorbing state of complete defection.
AI.conclusion: Reputation facilitates cooperation not only through direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

title: Climate change and human mobility will shape dengue emergence risk in Europe
summary: The risk of local arbovirus outbreaks in Europe is expected to increase due to climate change, as suggested by the multiplication of arbovirus outbreaks in the last decades. Europe has historically been a non-endemic region, making it vital to pinpoint which populations are potentially exposed -and under which conditions- so we can build truly robust epidemic preparedness capabilities. We introduce an integrated, multi-scale model that fuses a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework, all embedded in a mobility-driven metapopulation system capturing human, vector, and air-traffic movement. To this end, we combine climate and population projections with mobility data to estimate and map dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century. Additionally, we introduce a dedicated migration model that explores how climate-driven population redistribution could alter these risk estimates.Assuming the climate avoids major tipping points, model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios. While the spatio-temporal risk will remain largely driven by importation, our results indicate a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime, particularly under the worst-case emissions scenario. To better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks, our findings highlight the need to integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution into predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an integrated multi-scale model combining mechanistic transmission dynamics, vector abundance, and mobility-driven metapopulation systems to estimate dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century under various climate and emissions scenarios.
AI.motivation: Europe faces increasing arbovirus outbreak risk due to climate change, yet it has historically been non-endemic. Identifying potentially exposed populations and the conditions driving exposure is critical for building robust epidemic preparedness.
AI.method: The authors fuse a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework within a mobility-driven metapopulation system capturing human, vector, and air-traffic movement. They combine climate and population projections with mobility data, and introduce a dedicated migration model to explore how climate-driven population redistribution alters risk estimates.
AI.result: Assuming climate avoids major tipping points, model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios. Risk remains largely importation-driven in space and time, but a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime emerges, particularly under the worst-case emissions scenario.
AI.conclusion: Predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions must integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution to better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks.

title: Growth phases of an active tissue: determinate, indeterminate, and proportionate
summary: Growth may cease at a target size or continue throughout life: the determinate and indeterminate phenotypes. We develop an active viscoelastic continuum model of a tissue growing along one axis, in which cell division and death generate active stresses. We find two asymptotic states: one in which the tissue reaches a relative size fixed by its material parameters, and one in which it elongates linearly without bound. Which state is realised is set by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus. The transition originates in a bound on the elastic stress the tissue can support: a sufficiently large activity can never be balanced. In a tissue made of parts with different material properties, the growing phase settles into fixed length proportions, set by the mechanical impedances of the parts rather than inherited; matching impedances to initial lengths preserves the proportions the tissue began with. Determinate, indeterminate and proportionate growth thus appear as regimes of one continuum mechanical framework.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an active viscoelastic continuum model of tissue growth along one axis, showing that determinate (bounded) and indeterminate (unbounded linear) growth emerge as distinct regimes of the same framework, governed by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus, and that proportionate growth in heterogeneous tissues is set by mechanical impedance matching rather than inheritance.
AI.motivation: To unify determinate and indeterminate growth phenotypes within a single mechanical framework, and to understand how tissue proportions are established and maintained during growth.
AI.method: An active viscoelastic continuum model of tissue growing along one axis, where cell division and death generate active stresses; analysis of asymptotic growth states and transition conditions.
AI.result: Two asymptotic states emerge: fixed-size determinate growth and unbounded linear elongation. The realized state depends on the active stress-to-elastic modulus ratio, with a critical transition arising from a bound on supported elastic stress. In heterogeneous tissues, growing phases reach length proportions set by mechanical impedances, and matching impedances to initial lengths preserves initial proportions.
AI.conclusion: Determinate, indeterminate, and proportionate growth are not distinct mechanisms but emerge as regimes of one continuum mechanical framework.

title: Decoding silent reading from non-invasive EEG
comment: 45 pages (including 12 pages of Supplementary Material), 11 figures (including 2 in Supplementary Material)
summary: Non-invasive decoding of inner speech faces a fundamental data problem: a corpus pairing brain activity with a person's spontaneous inner monologue cannot be collected, and the available proxy paradigms (cued repetitive and retrospectively reported generative inner speech) are slow to acquire, poorly time-locked, and subject compliance is unverifiable. We therefore treat silent reading as a scalable proxy task and ask how much lexical and semantic information a contrastive decoder can extract from it. We report an open-vocabulary analysis of approximately 240,000 word presentations recorded from a single densely-sampled participant across 393 runs (ca. 49 h) of 19-channel dry-electrode EEG. Words from continuous narrative text were presented in rapid serial visual presentation, with typography randomised on every trial to partially decorrelate word identity from low-level visual form. A convolutional EEG encoder, optionally followed by a causal transformer, was trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective to align short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model. Decoding, evaluated as word-grouped top-10 retrieval against permutation baselines, was reliably above chance, extended to mid-frequency and rare words, and scaled log-linearly with training-data volume with no sign of saturation. Removing occipital and posterior-temporal electrodes reduced the word-level gain by roughly one third but left context tracking unchanged. Control analyses separate word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and from a non-neural positional prior introduced by the transformer's positional embedding. These results establish that open-vocabulary word-level information is recoverable from EEG during silent reading, and that decoding is data-limited rather than saturated.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that open-vocabulary word-level lexical and semantic information can be reliably decoded from 19-channel dry-electrode EEG during silent reading, using a CLIP-style contrastive decoder (convolutional encoder + optional causal transformer) trained on ~240,000 word presentations from a single participant across 49 hours. Decoding is above chance, scales log-linearly with data with no saturation, and partly depends on occipital/posterior-temporal electrodes, while control analyses separate word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and positional priors.
AI.motivation: Non-invasive inner speech decoding faces a fundamental data limitation: spontaneous inner monologue paired with brain activity cannot be collected, and proxy paradigms (cued repetitive, retrospectively reported generative speech) are slow, poorly time-locked, and have unverifiable compliance. The authors propose silent reading as a scalable proxy task to overcome this data bottleneck and investigate how much information can be recovered.
AI.method: One densely-sampled participant read continuous narrative text presented via rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) with randomized typography to decorrelate word identity from low-level visual form. A convolutional EEG encoder (optionally followed by a causal transformer) was trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective to align short EEG windows with large-language-model hidden-state embeddings of the presented word. Decoding was evaluated as word-grouped top-10 retrieval against permutation baselines.
AI.result: Reliable above-chance decoding was achieved, extending to mid-frequency and rare words, with log-linear scaling as training data increased and no sign of saturation. Removing occipital and posterior-temporal electrodes reduced word-level gain by ~1/3 but did not affect context tracking. Control analyses separated word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and from a positional prior from the transformer's positional embedding.
AI.conclusion: Open-vocabulary word-level information is recoverable from EEG during silent reading, and decoding performance is data-limited rather than saturated, suggesting that further improvements are possible with more training data.

title: GENIE: Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics
summary: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic highlighted the ongoing risk infectious diseases pose to society and the value of reliable information on the likely future burden. When forecasting an epidemic at fine spatial resolution, traditionally used mechanistic compartmental model struggle to capture highly complex granular transmission dynamics, resulting in inaccurate and overconfident forecasts. However, detailed Agent-Based Models (ABMs), are challenging to calibrate and are too computationally expensive to use in real-time. Amortized simulation-based inference promises to overcome this difficulty by exploiting the power of machine learning (ML) to perform approximate forecasting at near-real-time using arbitrarily complex models of epidemics. In this work we introduce Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics (GENIE), a spatio-temporal ML-based framework for high-resolution forecasting of the burden of respiratory pathogens. GENIE is designed to reflect two key characteristics of outbreaks: (i) shared biological mechanisms across locations and (ii) location-specific characteristics affecting transmission dynamics. This results in the model architecture having two modules: (i) a Local Infection Encoder - which learns to represent disease dynamics shared across all locations and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder - which learns location-specific representations. Using simulations from a high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM, GENIE is trained to generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution of future epidemic trajectories. Benchmarked against established statistical and ML models, GENIE demonstrates superior performance across a range of measures including the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.

AI.tldr: GENIE is a spatio-temporal machine learning framework that uses amortized simulation-based inference to produce near-real-time, high-resolution forecasts of respiratory pathogen epidemics, outperforming established statistical and ML baselines.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic compartmental models struggle with fine-grained spatial forecasting, while Agent-Based Models (ABMs) are too computationally expensive and hard to calibrate for real-time use, creating a need for a fast yet accurate forecasting approach.
AI.method: GENIE uses a two-module architecture: (i) a Local Infection Encoder to learn shared disease dynamics across locations, and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder to learn location-specific characteristics. The model is trained on simulations from a high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM to generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution of future epidemic trajectories.
AI.result: Benchmarked against established statistical and ML models, GENIE demonstrates superior performance across multiple measures, including accuracy in predicting the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.
AI.conclusion: Amortized simulation-based inference combined with deep learning can overcome the computational limitations of ABMs, enabling near-real-time, high-resolution epidemic forecasting that is both accurate and practical for real-world outbreak response.
